extracted.intended_audience: Recipients of Federal financial assistance (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, investigators, decision-makers, and institutional legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory standards and procedural requirements governing Title IX formal complaints and grievance processes, including evidence access, investigative reports, consolidation rules, privacy/FERPA interactions, employee applicability, notice, recordkeeping, and anti-retaliation requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to evidence and investigative report
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must provide parties and the party's advisor of choice with the evidence and investigative report in electronic format or a hard copy; a recipient may not refuse to provide the evidence or investigative report to a party's advisor if the party would like the advisor to have access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may provide hard copy access under supervision but cannot require that parties be denied copies to advisors. Verbal descriptions of evidence are insufficient because they may be inaccurate and fail to capture nuances. The regulation was revised (§106.45(b)(5)(vi)-(vii)) to allow electronic or hard copy provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative report content requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The investigative report must fairly summarize relevant evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients have discretion as to the contents of the investigative report; it may include facts and interview statements. If an investigator includes a credibility analysis, the investigator must avoid making a determination regarding responsibility because §106.45(b)(7)(i) prohibits the same person from being both investigator (or Title IX Coordinator) and decision-maker. The Department declined to be overly prescriptive about other components of the investigative report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on investigator as decision-maker / limits on credibility determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision-maker may not be the same person as the Title IX Coordinator or the investigator (§106.45(b)(7)(i)); investigators must be cautious that a credibility analysis does not amount to a determination regarding responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an investigator's credibility finding functions as a determination of responsibility, that would violate §106.45(b)(7)(i). Investigators may include credibility observations only so long as they do not usurp the decision-maker's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation of formal complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may consolidate formal complaints where the allegations of sexual harassment arise out of the same facts or circumstances (§106.45(b)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requirement for 'same facts and circumstances' means allegations are so intertwined they directly relate to all parties. If consolidated, parties must receive the same written determination regarding responsibility, simultaneously, and a recipient may not redact or withhold any part of the written determination. If not consolidated, separate written determinations must be issued for each formal complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties entitled to inspect and review directly related evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must be given an equal opportunity to inspect and review any evidence obtained as part of an investigation that is directly related to the allegations in a formal complaint, including evidence the recipient does not intend to rely on and inculpatory or exculpatory evidence (§106.45(b)(5)(vi)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A log of documents is not an adequate substitute for direct inspection because parties may not determine FERPA applicability or relevance from a log. Recipients have some discretion in determining what is 'directly related,' but the Department may find a violation if directly related evidence is withheld. Recipients may choose to log unproduced information to show both parties agreed it was not directly related, but no log is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy protections and methods of sharing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients have discretion to determine how privacy is best protected while complying with the regulations, but the Department does not require use of a specific platform that restricts downloading or copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department removed language that might be read to require file-sharing platforms that restrict downloading. Recipients may use platforms that limit copying/download, but they are not required to. Restrictions must still comply with the requirement to provide parties the opportunity to inspect/review directly related evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment/medical records access restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient is restricted from accessing, considering, disclosing, or otherwise using a party's treatment records (records made or maintained by a physician, psychiatrist, psychologist, or other recognized professional or paraprofessional in connection with treatment) unless the recipient obtains the party's voluntary, written consent for the grievance process (§106.45(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the party is not an 'eligible student' under FERPA, the recipient must obtain the voluntary, written consent of a 'parent' as defined in 34 CFR 99.3. If a complainant does not provide those records or consent, the respondent cannot inspect them as part of the grievance process.

rubrics_metrics.name: FERPA interaction and redaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether FERPA applies to records obtained during a §106.45 grievance process depends on circumstances; FERPA may require redaction of information not directly related to allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients are not required to share information that is not directly related to a formal complaint and FERPA may preclude disclosure of personally identifiable education records without consent. Recipients may redact documents when redactions are consistent with providing due process and not relevant to the proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police investigation files and social media evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may make police investigation files available to parties if those files contain evidence directly related to the allegations; recipients may use lawfully obtained social media profiles as part of the investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department does not require specific technical platforms to share information and will continue to provide technical assistance. Lawful acquisition is a precondition to using social media content in investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement against substituting a document log for evidence access
rubrics_metrics.description: A log of all documents is not sufficient in place of providing parties with the actual evidence directly related to allegations, because parties need to respond to evidence prior to completion of the investigative report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may not always determine from a log alone whether a record is an education record or whether FERPA prohibits disclosure. The purpose of providing evidence is to allow parties to respond and help ensure a fair and accurate investigative report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record retention requirement (seven years)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must retain grievance process records for seven years under §106.45(b)(10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This seven-year retention does not conflict with FERPA, which does not mandate a specific retention period, and recipients must not destroy records if there is an outstanding request to inspect/review. A destruction requirement at end of grievance could violate Clery Act recordkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-disclosure agreements and confidentiality limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may require restrictions or use non-disclosure agreements for confidential information so long as doing so does not violate these regulations or other applicable laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations do not define the universe of confidential information; recipients are in a better position to identify and protect confidential records. The retaliation provision (§106.71) does not specifically address confidential documents, but using confidential documents for retaliation is prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of written notice of hearings and meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(5)(v) requires a recipient to provide the party whose participation is invited or expected written notice of the date, time, location, participants, and purpose of all hearings, investigative interviews, or other meetings with a party, with sufficient time for the party to prepare to participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This written notice requirement applies equally to employees and students; nothing precludes providing such notice to employees in the grievance process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of grievance procedures to employees
rubrics_metrics.description: The grievance process in §106.45 applies to any person—students or employees—who experiences sexual harassment in an education program or activity of a recipient of Federal financial assistance; definitions in §106.30 apply to all of 34 CFR part 106.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must handle formal complaints of sexual harassment under §106.45 irrespective of whether complainant or respondent is a student or employee. Nothing in part 106 may be read in derogation of any individual's rights under Title VII (§106.6(f)); recipients may also enforce separate codes of conduct that go beyond Title IX requirements. Mandatory dismissal under §106.45(b)(3)(i) is only for Title IX purposes and does not preclude action under other provisions of the recipient's code of conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate indifference standard under Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department adopts the deliberate indifference standard in §106.44(a) as the appropriate Title IX standard for recipients' responses to sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains that this standard is appropriate in educational contexts to avoid undue restrictions on speech, conduct, and academic freedom; it differs from standards under Title VII and prior guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory dismissal scope and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(3)(i) requires mandatory dismissal of formal complaints in certain circumstances (e.g., conduct not meeting the §106.30 definition or outside program/activity); such a dismissal does not preclude enforcement of non-Title IX conduct rules by the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recipient may still apply its own code of conduct to address misconduct that does not meet Title IX's definition or that occurred outside the United States; the regulation clarifies dismissal is only for Title IX purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-retaliation prohibition (§106.71)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department added §106.71 to expressly prohibit retaliation: no recipient or other person may intimidate, threaten, coerce, or discriminate against any individual for the purpose of interfering with any right or privilege secured by Title IX or these regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision also clarifies that exercising rights protected under the First Amendment does not constitute retaliation, but threatening to publicize a written determination for the purpose of retaliation is prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope clarifications across part 106
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department revised §106.30 so that, aside from the definitions of 'elementary and secondary school' and 'postsecondary institution,' the definitions in §106.30 apply to the entirety of 34 CFR part 106 (not just subpart D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change clarifies that the definitions used for sexual harassment and related terms are applicable across regulatory subparts, helping recipients determine applicability and process handling.
